stem: In the physics lab, Sneha hangs two pendulums with equal string lengths. Bob X is 50 g and is pulled to 3°; bob Y is 200 g and is pulled to 6° (both small). She releases them together. Which finishes 10 oscillations first?

options.A: X, because its swing is smaller so each oscillation is shorter
options.B: Y, because gravity pulls the heavier bob harder so it swings faster
options.D: X, because the lighter bob is easier to move back and forth

r1.text: Y swings through a bigger arc, so it has more distance to cover and takes more time.

r2.text: T = 2π√(L/g) has only length and g in it, and both have the same length, so the period is the same.

r3.text: The heavy bob gets pulled down with more force, so it comes back quicker.

calc: T = 2π√(L/g) for both; independent of bob mass and of small amplitude, so both finish 10 oscillations together.
verify_flags: Assumes negligible air drag on both bobs and both angles within the small-angle regime.

stem: Rohan's simple pendulum is 0.64 m long and swings with an amplitude of 3°. He restarts it at 6° (still small). Take g = π² m/s². What is the time period now?

r1.text: He doubled the swing, so the bob travels double the path and the period doubles too.

r2.text: Amplitude isn't in T = 2π√(L/g), so the period stays what it was for 3°.

r3.text: ω = √(g/L) and the period is just 1/ω, so I take one by omega.

stem: An empty tempo bounces on its suspension springs with a period of 0.5 s. After loading sacks of onions at a Nashik market, its total mass becomes 4 times. Treating it as a spring–mass system, what is the new bounce period?

options.B: 0.5 s, because the springs, not the load, decide the period
options.D: 0.5 s on a smooth road, but longer when a speed breaker makes it bounce higher

r1.text: T = 2π√(m/k), so 4 times the mass gives √4 = 2 times the period.

r2.text: Mass only matters for weight; the bounce time depends on how stiff the spring is.

r3.text: A bigger bounce means the tempo goes up and down more, so it takes more time.

calc: T ∝ √m: T₂ = 0.5 × √4 = 1.0 s. SLIP (T ∝ m, forgot root): 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 s.
verify_flags: Real vehicle suspension has dampers and non-ideal springs; idealised as a single spring–mass system with k unchanged.

stem: Kavya's spring–mass system oscillates with angular frequency 4π rad/s at an amplitude of 5 cm. She pulls the block to 10 cm and releases it. What is the frequency of oscillation now?

r1.text: Frequency is the same thing as omega here, so it is 4π, about 12.6 Hz.

r2.text: f = ω/2π = 2 Hz, and amplitude doesn't change ω for a spring, so it stays 2 Hz.

r3.text: Double the stretch means double the distance, so the period doubles and frequency halves.

calc: f = ω/2π = 4π/2π = 2 Hz, independent of amplitude. S10: f = ω = 4π ≈ 12.6 Hz. S8: T doubled from 0.5 s to 1.0 s → 1 Hz. UNMAPPED: reported T = 0.5 s as 0.5 Hz.

stem: Meera swaps her pendulum's brass bob for a heavier iron bob of the same size, keeps the string length the same, and pulls it a little further (still a small angle). Does the period change? Why?
answer_key: No, the period stays the same because T = 2π√(L/g) depends only on length and g.
expected_reasoning: For small angles the pendulum's period depends only on L and g; the bob's mass cancels out and amplitude does not appear in the formula.

follow_ups.S8: If the bob is pulled further, it has a longer path. What else changes about how fast it moves at the bottom?
follow_ups.S9: In T = 2π√(L/g), where would the bob's mass appear? What happens to m when you write F = ma for the bob?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: You said the period does not change. Which quantities does a simple pendulum's period actually depend on?
follow_ups.CORRECT: Meera now takes the same pendulum to a hill station where g is slightly smaller. Will the period increase, decrease or stay the same?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Will one oscillation of the new bob take more time, less time, or the same time as before?

verify_flags: Same-size bob chosen so air drag is comparable; real heavy vs light bobs differ slightly due to drag.

stem: A spring toy on Aditya's desk oscillates with angular frequency 10π rad/s. What is its time period? Give your value with the formula you used.
expected_reasoning: Angular frequency ω is 2π times the frequency, so T = 2π/ω, not 1/ω; this gives f = 5 Hz and T = 0.2 s.

slips.why: used T = 1/ω, treating ω as the frequency
gave the frequency f = 5 Hz instead of the period

follow_ups.S10: ω is measured in rad/s and f in oscillations per second. How many radians does the block go through in one full oscillation?
follow_ups.S9: The mass and spring constant decide ω. If ω is already given, do you still need m to find T?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: You got 0.2 s. Why do we divide 2π by ω instead of just taking 1/ω?
follow_ups.CORRECT: If the same toy is given a block of 4 times the mass, what will its new angular frequency be?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Please give one number in seconds for the time of one full oscillation.

verify_flags: Check that the grader's numeric tolerance (0.01 s) does not swallow the 0.032 s slip; it does not at |0.2 − 0.032|.

stem: A block on a spring has a time period of 1.2 s. Anjali replaces it with a block 4 times as heavy on the same spring. What happens to the period, and why?
answer_key: The period doubles to 2.4 s because T = 2π√(m/k) and √4 = 2.
expected_reasoning: For a spring–mass system T = 2π√(m/k), so the period is proportional to √m; four times the mass gives twice the period.

follow_ups.S9: A heavier block feels the same spring force but has more inertia. Will it speed up and slow down more quickly or more slowly than the light one?
follow_ups.S8: Nothing was said about how far the block is pulled. Does T = 2π√(m/k) contain the amplitude at all?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: Why does 4 times the mass give 2 times the period and not 4 times?
follow_ups.CORRECT: Anjali wants the heavy block to have a period of 1.2 s again. By what factor must she change the spring constant?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Will the new period be longer, shorter or equal to 1.2 s? Say by how much.

verify_flags: accept_any 'double' also matches 'doubled'; a student writing 'not double' would be mis-graded.
